en: Dharmakīrti: The Sūtra Text of the *Nyāyabindu-prakaraṇakārikā*
Chapter One: Direct Perception (Pratyakṣa).
1/1 Since the accomplishment of all human goals is preceded by right knowledge, that [knowledge] is here explained.
1/2 Right knowledge is of two kinds.
1/3 Perception and inference. 1/4 Among these, perception is that which is free from conceptual construction and non-erroneous.

1/5 Conceptualization (*kalpanā*) is the cognition of an appearance that is capable of being associated with verbal expression. 1/6 Direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is cognition devoid of that [conceptualization], free from the delusions induced by such causes as cataracts, rapid spinning, traveling in a boat, or agitation. 1/7 It is of four kinds.
(1) Sensory cognition (*indriyajñāna*).

(2) Mental cognition (*manovijñāna*) is that which is produced by sensory cognition acting as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), with the assistance of the object immediately following its own [sensory] object.
(3) Self-awareness (*ātmasaṃvedana*) of all minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).
(4) 1/11 And there is the yogic cognition produced from the ultimate limit of the intensification of the cultivation of the real object.
1/12 Its object is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
1/13 That object whose manifestation in cognition differs according to its presence or absence is the particular characteristic.
1/14 That alone is ultimately real;
1/15 because a functional thing is characterized by its capacity for causal efficiency;
1/16 anything else is a general characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa).

1/17 That [inference] is the object of inference. 1/18 And for this very reason, direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is the fruit of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because it consists in the cognition of the object.
1/19 Because its nature is the apprehension of the object.
The conformity of this [cognition] with the object is its means of valid cognition (pramāṇa),
because the establishment of the cognition of the object occurs by virtue of that [conformity].
Thus ends the first chapter, on direct perception (pratyakṣa).
The second chapter: Inference for Oneself.
Inference is of two kinds:
for oneself and for others.
2/3 Therein, inference is that cognition which, based on a mark possessing the three characteristics, occurs with respect to the object of inference.
2/4 The establishment of the definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) here is also as before.
2/5 Furthermore, the three characteristics of the mark are: its existence only in the object of inference;
Existence only in the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and non-existence only in the dissimilar class (*asapakṣa*) are certain.
Here, the "object of inference" (*anumeya*) is the locus (*dharmin*) whose specific property one desires to know. 2/6.
2/7 A similar instance (sapakṣa) is an object that is similar by virtue of possessing the general property to be proven (sādhyadharma).

2/8 A non-similar instance (asapakṣa) is that which is not a similar instance. 2/9 This [non-similar instance] consists of that which is other than it, that which is contradictory to it, and the absence of it.
2/10 Furthermore, there are exactly three types of logical marks (*liṅga*) characterized by the three forms [of the reason].
2/11 These are non-perception (*anupalabdhi*), essential nature (*svabhāva*), and effect (*kārya*).
2/12 Among these, non-perception is as follows: for example, "there is no jar in a particular location."
"Because there is no perception of that which has reached the conditions for perception" (2.13).
"Reaching the conditions for perception" consists in the completeness of all other causal factors for perception and a specific nature (svabhāva) [of the object] (2.14).
That nature which, when the other causal factors for perception are present, becomes directly perceived—
That is the distinction of essential nature (*svabhāvaviśeṣa*).
An essential nature is a reason (*hetu*) when the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is produced solely by its own existence.
For example: "This is a tree because it is a *śiṃśapā*."
2/17 An example of an effect [as a reason] is: "There is fire here because there is smoke.
2/18 Here, two [reasons] establish a positive entity, while one is a reason for negation.

For when there is an essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*), one object (*artha*) may lead to the cognition of another object; because for that which is not so connected, there is no necessity of non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) from it. And that connection belongs to the mark (*liṅga*) with respect to the object to be proven (*sādhya*).
2/22 Because [the object] is in fact identical with it (*tādātmya*) and because it arises from it (*tadutpatti*).
2/23 Because that which does not have that nature (*atatsvabhāva*) does not arise from it, since its nature is not necessarily connected to it.
2/24 And since those two—identity and origination—belong only to essential nature (*svabhāva*) and effect (*kārya*), the establishment of a real entity (*vastu*) occurs through these two alone.
2/25 The establishment of a negation also proceeds from non-apprehension exactly as described;
2/26 because that [non-apprehension] is impossible when a thing exists;

2/27 and otherwise, because there would be no certainty regarding the absence of things remote in space, time, or nature—even though they meet the conditions for non-apprehension—due to the mere cessation of one's own perception.
2/28 The cessation of the cognizer’s direct perception—whether past (whose impressions of memory are not confused) or present—is that which establishes the conventional usage of non-existence.
2/29 This is because it is from that very [cessation] that the determination of non-existence arises.
2/30 And that [non-existence] is of eleven types due to the differences in its application.

2/31 Non-perception of the essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*), for example: "There is no smoke here, because [smoke] that has reached the conditions for perception is not perceived. (1) 2/32 Non-perception of the effect (*kāryānupalabdhi*), for example: "The causes of smoke, whose capacities are unimpeded, do not exist here, because smoke is absent. (2)

2/33 Non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) is, for example: "There is no *śiṃśapā* tree here, because there is no tree. (3) 2/34 Perception of what is incompatible with the essential nature (*svabhāvaviruddhopalabdhi*) is, for example: "There is no sensation of cold here, because of fire. (4)
2/35 Perception of a contradictory effect (*viruddhakāryopalabdhi*): for example, "There is no sensation of cold here, because of smoke.

(5) 2/36 Perception of what is pervaded by the contradictory (*viruddhavyāptopalabdhi*): for example, "The destruction of even an existing entity is not necessarily certain, because it depends on other causes. (6)
2/37 Perception of that which is incompatible with the effect (*kāryaviruddhopalabdhi*): for example, "There are no causes of cold here possessing unimpeded capacity, because of fire.
(7) 2/38 Perception of that which is incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*): for example, "There is no touch of frost here, because of fire.
(8) 2/39 Non-perception of the cause (*kāraṇānupalabdhi*): for example, "There is no smoke here, because of the absence of fire. (9)

2/40 Perception of what is incompatible with the cause (*kāraṇaviruddhopalabdhi*), for example: "He does not possess specific qualities such as horripilation, because there is a specific fire present nearby. (10) 2/41 Perception of what is incompatible with the effect of the cause (*kāraṇaviruddhakāryopalabdhi*), for example: "This place does not contain a person possessed of specific qualities such as horripilation, because there is smoke. (11)

2/42 All these ten applications of non-apprehension, beginning with the non-apprehension of the effect (*kāryānupalabdhi*), are included within the non-apprehension of the essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*).
2/43 This is because, although there is a difference in application due to the affirmation or negation of other things through a mediated sequence, [they all ultimately reduce to it].

2/44 Through the practice of observing these applications, one comes to personally understand such exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) even in inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*); therefore, its application is here set forth.

2/45 Furthermore, in this non-apprehension which establishes the conventional usage of absence, those things— such as the perception of what is contradictory to their own nature (*svabhāvaviruddha*) or the non-apprehension of causes (*kāraṇa*) and so forth— for whose negation it has been stated, must be understood as being subject to non-apprehension because they have met the conditions for perceptibility (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*).
2/46 This is because for other things, the relationship of contradiction, effect, or cause is not established.
Furthermore, non-apprehension whose object is remote is characterized by the cessation of perception and inference, and it is a cause of doubt;
for even when the means of valid cognition have ceased, the non-existence of the object is not established.
Thus ends the second chapter, the Investigation of Inference for Oneself.
The third chapter: On Inference for Others (Parārthānumāna).
3/1 Inference for others is the communication of a logical mark (liṅga) possessing the three characteristics.
3/2 This is because the term for the effect is metaphorically applied to its cause.
3/3 That [inference] is of two kinds;
3/4 because of the difference in its application;
3/5 namely, that which possesses similarity and that which possesses dissimilarity.
3/6 There is no difference between these two in terms of their meaning;
3/7 they differ only in their mode of application (prayoga).

3/8 Among them, the formulation based on similarity (sādharmya) is as follows: that which, having met the conditions for perceptibility, is not perceived, is established as being the object of the conventional usage of "non-existent."
For example: something else, such as a hare's horn, has been seen;
yet a jar, though meeting the conditions for perception, is not perceived in any particular location—this is the formulation of non-perception (*anupalabdhi*).
(3/9) Similarly, the formulation of the reason of essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*) is: whatever exists, all that is impermanent.
"Just as a jar, etc. is the formulation of a pure essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*).
"Whatever has origination is impermanent" is the formulation of an essential nature (*svabhāva*) by way of a distinction within that which constitutes its own nature.
"Whatever is produced is impermanent" is [the formulation] by way of a distinction in limiting conditions (*upādhi*).
3/12 For a thing (*bhāva*) that requires the operation of another for the production of its own nature (*svabhāva*) is called "produced" (*kṛtaka*).

3/13 In the same way, [reasons] such as "being preceded by effort" (*prayatnāntarīyakatva*) and "varying according to the difference in conditions" (*pratyayabhedabheditva*) are also to be understood.
3/14 "Sound is existent, produced, or created" is the demonstration of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*).

3/15 All these properties of the probans (sādhanadharma) are to be understood as being invariably concomitant with the property to be proven (sādhyadharma) solely through the establishment of that probandum-property by its respective means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
3/16 This is because that [probandum] has that very [probans] as its intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
3/17 And because the intrinsic nature itself serves as the logical reason (hetu).
3/18 In reality, there is identity between those two.
3/19 Because that which is not yet produced when the other is produced lacks the nature of being identical to it.
3/20 And because deviation is possible.
The application of the reason based on effect (kāryahetu): Wherever there is smoke, there is fire, as in the kitchen and so forth;
and here there is smoke.
3/22 Here too, only when the relationship of cause and effect is already established may the "effect-reason" (kāryahetu) be stated when the cause is to be proven.
3/23 The formulation by way of dissimilarity (vaidharmya): Whatever exists and meets the conditions for perception is necessarily perceived, just as a particular such as blue and so forth.

And thus, in this case, there is no application of non-apprehension [as a reason], because a jar that has reached the conditions for apprehension is not apprehended. If impermanence were non-existent,
then existence, the state of having an origin, or being produced would not exist.
"Sound is existent, produced, or created"—this is the application of a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
"Where there is no fire, smoke does not exist at all;
yet here there is smoke"—this is the application of a reason based on effect (*kāryahetu*).
For even in an argument based on similarity (sādharmya), the understanding of dissimilarity (vaidharmya) follows by implication;

because in its absence, there would be no positive concomitance (anvaya) of the reason with the probandum. Likewise, even in an argument based on dissimilarity, the understanding of positive concomitance follows.
3/29 Because, in the absence of that [invariable concomitance], the non-existence of the reason (*hetu*) when the probandum (*sādhya*) is absent is not established.
3/30 For, when there is no essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*), the necessary cessation of one thing upon the cessation of another does not occur.
3/31 And that [essential connection] is of two kinds—as it has been stated: characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) and characterized by origination from that (*tadutpatti*).
Therefore, one who states an absence (nivṛtti) must demonstrate the necessary connection (pratibandha).
Consequently, the statement of an absence is nothing other than the demonstration of the implied connection;

and that demonstration of the connection is itself the statement of positive concomitance (anvaya). Thus, even by a single sentence—whether by way of positive concomitance or by way of negative concomitance—[the relationship is established].

Or, since the presence and absence of the logical mark (*liṅga*) in the similar and dissimilar instances has been made known by the employment [of the first statement], the employment of two statements is not strictly necessary.
(3.33) Regarding non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) as well: when it is stated that "whatever exists and meets the conditions for apprehension is necessarily apprehended," [the point is established].
The establishment of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is based on the cognition that such a thing, when not being perceived, is non-existent.
(3/34) In both of these formulations, the explicit mention of the subject (*pakṣa*) is not strictly necessary.
(3/35) For even in the formulation characterized by similarity (*sādharmyavat*), [the meaning is conveyed by] "that which, though meeting the conditions for perceptibility, is not perceived."
That is the object of the conventional usage of "non-existent.
When it is stated, "And here, a jar meeting the conditions for perception is not perceived," it follows by implication that "there is no jar here.

(3.36) Likewise, in the formulation characterized by dissimilarity (*vaidharmyavat-prayoga*) as well: whatever is an object of the conventional usage of "existent" and meets the conditions for perception is necessarily perceived.
When it is said, "In this case, such a jar is not perceived," it follows by implication alone that it is not an object of the conventional usage of existence here.
(3/37) But what kind of thesis (*pakṣa*) is to be specified? (3/38) A thesis is that which is intended by [the proponent] himself in its own form and is not refuted.
3/39 "By its own nature" (svarūpeṇa) means intended as that which is to be proven (sādhya).
3/40 "Only by its own nature" (svarūpeṇaiva) means intended solely as that which is to be proven, and not even as a means of proof (sādhana).
3/41 For example, when the impermanence of sound is to be proven, visibility (cākṣuṣatva) is [not a valid] reason (hetu).

Because it is unestablished (*asiddha*) with respect to the word, it is something to be proven (*sādhya*); however, it is not intended here solely as that which is to be proven, since it is also expressed as a means of proof (*sādhana*).
[The term] "himself" (*svayam*) refers to the proponent (*vādin*).
3/43–44: Regarding the one who states the proof (*sādhana*) at that time:

although he may state the proof while adhering to a particular treatise (*śāstra*), even though the author of that treatise may have accepted many properties (*dharma*) regarding that subject (*dharmin*), it has been stated that only that property which the proponent himself intends to prove at that time is the *sādhya* (the thing to be proven), and no other.
It is so.

(3/45) Regarding the term "desired" (*iṣṭa*): when a proof (*sādhana*) is presented in connection with a certain object that is subject to dispute, that object becomes the probandum (*sādhya*) even if it is not explicitly stated by words, provided one desires its establishment.
(3/46) This is because the dispute has that very object as its basis.
Just as the eyes and so forth exist for the sake of another because they are composite, like the parts of a bed or a seat;
in this case, even though "for the sake of a self" is not explicitly stated, it is precisely "being for the sake of a self" that is to be proven.
Thus, it is shown that it is not merely what has been stated [in the reason] that constitutes the probandum.

3/48 Regarding the term "not set aside" (*anirākṛta*): this is for the purpose of demonstrating that even when a subject possesses these defining characteristics, if the intended object to be proven is nevertheless contradicted by perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), common consensus (*pratīti*), or one's own words (*svavacana*), it does not constitute a valid thesis (*pakṣa*).
3/49 Among these, an example of what is set aside by perception is: "Sound is inaudible. (1)
(1) An example of that which is refuted by inference (*anumānanirākṛta*) is: "Sound is eternal.
(2) An example of that which is refuted by common cognition (*pratītinirākṛta*) is: "The moon is not the moon (*acandra*).
(3) An example of that which is refuted by one's own words (*svavacananirākṛta*) is: "Inference is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). (4) [End of section]
Thus, four fallacious positions (pakṣābhāsa) are refuted.

Likewise, [the following are also excluded]: that which is already established, that which is not yet established despite being intended as a means of proof (sādhana), and that which the proponent himself does not intend to prove at that time.

"The thesis (*pakṣa*) is that which is intended by the proponent in its very nature, is desired [by him], and is not refuted"— by this, the faultless definition of the thesis is shown, [namely] that it is the opposite of what has been merely stated and what has been refuted.

3/55 It has been stated that inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*) is the communication of a logical mark (*liṅga*) possessing three characteristics (*trirūpa*). In this regard, if even one of the three characteristics is not stated, it is a fallacy of the proof (*sādhanābhāsa*).
3/56 Even if they are stated, if there is non-establishment (*asiddhi*) or doubt (*sandeha*) regarding them for either the person being instructed or the instructor, [it is likewise a fallacy].
3/57 An unestablished reason (*asiddha-hetvābhāsa*) is one that is unestablished or doubtful with respect to its connection with the subject (*dharmin*) of a single property.
3/58 For example, when "sound is impermanent" is the thesis to be proven (*sādhya*), "visibility" (*cākṣuṣatva*) is unestablished for both [proponent and opponent].
3/59 When "trees are sentient" is the thesis to be proven, death resulting from the removal of all bark is unestablished for the opponent.

Because death, characterized by the cessation of consciousness, the sense faculties, and vitality, is accepted [as the subject] by this [proponent], and because that [cessation] is impossible in trees;
[and] because "possessing the quality of being produced" is [the reason] when "pleasure and so forth are insentient" is the probandum. 3/60.
For the Sāṃkhya proponent, impermanence itself is unestablished (asiddha).
Likewise, there is non-establishment when there is doubt regarding its own basis.
For example, a collection of elements that is suspected of being steam or the like, yet is presented for the purpose of proving fire, is "unestablished due to doubt" (sandigdhāsiddha).
3/63 Just as [one infers] "there is a peacock here in this bower" from its cry;
3/64 that is [an example of] fallacy regarding confusion about the location of the manifestation.

3/65 It is also unestablished when the locus itself is unestablished—for example, when it is to be proven that "the self is omnipresent," the reason "having qualities perceived everywhere" is unestablished.

3/66 Likewise, when the absence of the probans from the dissimilar instances (*asapakṣa*)—which is one of its essential characteristics—is unestablished, it is a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) characterized by being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

3/67 For example, when a property such as impermanence is to be proven of sound, a property such as "being cognizable" (*prameyatva*) exists in all or part of both the similar (*sapakṣa*) and dissimilar instances. 3/68 Similarly, even when there is doubt regarding this very characteristic, it is likewise inconclusive.

3/69 For example, when the property to be proven (*sādhya*) is that "a certain intended person is omniscient" or "possesses a king and so forth," a property such as "being a speaker" (*vaktṛtva*) has a doubtful exclusion from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*).
3/70 This is because a non-perception (*anupalambha*) of the form "an omniscient speaker is not perceived" serves as a cause for doubt, since its object is an invisible nature;
therefore, the exclusion of "being a speaker" and the like from the opposite of "non-omniscience" is itself doubtful.

3/71 Furthermore, because there is no contradiction between being a speaker and being omniscient, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—that "whoever is omniscient is not a speaker"—is not established even in the absence of observation, due to doubt.
3/72 For the contradiction between entities is of two kinds.
3/73 The understanding of contradiction arises from the non-existence of something that possesses its complete causes when another thing exists.
3/74 Like the sensations of cold and heat;
3/75 Or like existence and non-existence, by virtue of having the characteristic of existing through mutual exclusion;
3/76 And neither of these two types of contradiction is possible between the states of being a speaker and being omniscient.
3/77 Furthermore, even when there is non-perception, there is no comprehension of absence through a rule that is not contradictory [to the presence of the object].
3/78 This is because the causal relationship between passion and the like and speech and the like has not been established.
3/79 Moreover, upon the cessation of something else that is not its cause, there is no cessation of speech and the like.
3/80 Thus, speech and the like are inconclusive (anaikāntika) because their negative concomitance (vyatireka) is doubtful.
3/81 When the two forms [of the reason] are established as the reverse [of what they should be], it is contradictory (viruddha). 3/82 Of which two?
3/83 [This refers to] the presence in the similar class (sapakṣa) and the absence in the dissimilar class (asapakṣa).
For example, "being produced" and "being immediately subsequent to effort" are contradictory fallacious reasons (viruddha-hetvābhāsa) when proving permanence.
3/84. In these two cases, there is non-existence in the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and existence in the dissimilar class (*asapakṣa*); thus, there is the establishment of the opposite.
3/85. And these two are contradictory (*viruddha*) because they prove the opposite of the probandum (*sādhya*).
3/86 But is not the third type also a contradictory reason (*viruddha*) because it thwarts what is intended?
3/87 For example: "The eyes and other [senses] exist for the sake of another (*parārtha*), because they are composite (*saṅghātatva*), like beds, seats, and other [composite] objects.
3/88 This is a contradictory reason because it proves the opposite of the intended non-composite nature of being for the sake of another.
3/89 Why is this not mentioned here?
3/90 Because it is included within these two very [categories].
3/91 For this does not differ from those two by way of proving the opposite of what is to be proven (*sādhyaviparyaya*).
3/92 There is no distinction whatsoever between what is desired and what is stated by way of being the probandum (*sādhya*).
3/93 When one of two characteristics is unestablished and the other is doubtful, it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
3/94 For example: "Someone is free from passion, or else he is omniscient."
Regarding the reason "because of being a speaker":
here, the negative concomitance (vyatireka) is unestablished,
and the positive concomitance (anvaya) is doubtful.
3/95 Because an omniscient being and one free from passion are beyond perception, the existence or non-existence of [qualities] such as speech in them is doubtful.
3/96 When there is doubt regarding these very two forms [of the probans], it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
3/97 For example: "The living body possesses a self (*sātmaka*), because it possesses breath and so forth."
3/98 For there exists no other category apart from those possessing a self (*sātmaka*) and those lacking a self (*nirātmaka*) wherein this [set of] vital breaths and so forth could reside.
3/99 Because everything is subsumed within these two categories by way of either the presence or the exclusion of the activity of a self.
3/100 Nor is there any certainty regarding the presence [of the vital breaths] in one or the other of these two.
3/101 Because [the reason] such as breath is unestablished with respect to [the subject] being established either as possessing a self (*sātmaka*) or as lacking a self (*anātmaka*).

3/102 Therefore, since breath and so forth, which are related to a living body, are unestablished by virtue of being excluded from everything—both that which possesses a self and that which lacks a self—they are not distinct from those two; 3/103 nor do they follow through them.
3/104 Because it is not established even in a single instance of the self.
3/105 Nor can there be a determination of the absence of its positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) with both that which possesses a self and that which lacks a self;
3/106 because the determination of the absence of one is inseparable from the determination of the presence of the other.

3/107 Because positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) consist in their mutual exclusion, it follows that due to doubt regarding these two concomitances, the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
3/108 This is because there is consequently no certainty regarding either the probandum (*sādhya*) or its opposite.

3/109 Thus, when each one of these three forms [of the reason] is unestablished (*asiddha*), or when two of them are unestablished, or when there is doubt regarding them, there are, as the case may be, the three fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*): the unestablished, the contradictory (*viruddha*), and the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
3/110 It has been stated that the "non-deviating contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārī*) is also a cause for doubt;
why then is it not mentioned here?
3/111 Because [contradiction] is impossible within the domain of inference.
3/112 For there is no possibility of contradiction between the effect (*kārya*) and the essential nature (*svabhāva*)—as defined above—and non-perception (*anupalambha*).
3/113 Nor is there any other [reason] that is non-deviant (*avyabhicārin*).

Therefore, relying upon an inference based on scripture—which functions by the power of perceiving what is non-existent—a "contradictory non-erroneous" (viruddhāvyabhicārī) probans is stated as a fault in the investigation of its objects.
This is because it is possible for authors of treatises to erroneously attribute a contrary nature to things;
however, such a possibility does not exist regarding the actual state of things as they are established, namely, in the case of essential natures, effects, and non-perceptions.
3/117 An example of this is as follows: that which is simultaneously related to its own correlates situated in all locations is omnipresent (*sarvagata*), just like space (*ākāśa*).
And the universal (*sāmānya*) is simultaneously related to its own correlates situated in all locations.
3/118 The state of being present in that location is necessarily concomitant with the mere nature of being related to that [object].
3/119 For it is not the case that what does not exist in a certain place pervades that place by its own nature; such is the application of the essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*).
3/120 The second formulation is as follows: whatever, having met the conditions for perception, is not perceived, does not exist there.
For example: a jar is non-existent in some places;
and a universal that has met the conditions for perception is not perceived in the intervals between individual instances.
This non-perception (*anupalambha*) and the essential nature (*svabhāva*) [of the universal] produce doubt regarding a single locus because they establish mutually contradictory meanings.

The reason has been stated as having three characteristics (*trirūpa*). Since the comprehension of the object is achieved by that much alone, there is no separate member of the proof called the "example" (*dṛṣṭānta*).
Therefore, its definition is not stated separately, because its purpose is already encompassed [by the definition of the reason].
The nature of the reason has been stated without distinction as its presence only in the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and its exclusion from the dissimilar class (*asapakṣa*) in all respects.

Furthermore, with respect to the specific [reasons]—namely, the effect and the essential nature whose characteristics have already been stated—their birth and their necessary concomitance with that alone are said to be shown.
And demonstrating that: "Wherever there is smoke, there is fire."
Just as there is no smoke anywhere in the absence of fire, whether in a kitchen or elsewhere;

so it should be shown that where there is "being produced" (kṛtakatva), there is "impermanence" (anityatva), and where impermanence is absent, "being produced" is impossible, as in the case of a jar and space.
For otherwise, the presence and absence of the reason in the similar and dissimilar instances could not be demonstrated in the manner described.
This refers to the restriction of being an effect for the effect-reason (*kāryaliṅga*),
and for the essential-nature reason (*svabhāvaliṅga*), it is the pervasion by its own nature.
And when this point has been demonstrated, the examples have already been demonstrated as well,
because they consist of nothing more than this;
by this very fact, the defects of the examples are also refuted.
3/124 For example: "Sound is eternal because it is incorporeal, like action, like an atom, and like a jar.
These are fallacious examples (dṛṣṭāntābhāsa), being deficient in the property to be proven (sādhya), the proving property (sādhana), or both.
Likewise, there are cases where the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) and so forth are doubtful.
For example: "This person possesses passion and the like, because he speaks, like a man on the street";
or, "This person is subject to death, because he possesses passion and the like, like a man on the street."
"This person is not omniscient because he possesses passion and other defilements, like a man in the street"—
this [reason] is likewise either lacking positive concomitance (*ananvaya*) or having its positive concomitance (*anvaya*) unshown. 3/126.
For example: "Whoever is a speaker possesses passion and so forth, like a person under consideration";
and "Sound is impermanent because it is produced, like a jar."
3/127 Likewise, there is the inverted positive concomitance (*viparītānvaya*): "Whatever is impermanent is produced. 3/128 These are the faults of the example by way of similarity (*sādharmya*).

3/129 Also by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*): [the examples] "like an atom," "like action," and "like space" are those that lack the exclusion of the probandum and so forth (*sādhyādyavyatirekin*).
Likewise, there are cases where the exclusion of the probandum (*sādhyavyatireka*) and so forth are doubtful.

For example: "Kapila and others are not omniscient or are non-authoritative (*anāpta*), because they do not possess a teaching characterized by a preeminent means of valid cognition (*pramāṇātiśaya*) that serves as a mark for the existence of omniscience or authoritativeness.
Here, the example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyodāharaṇa*) is: "Whoever is omniscient or authoritative has taught [matters such as] the knowledge of astrology (*jyotirjñāna*) and so forth."
For example: "such as Ṛṣabha, Vardhamāna, and others.
In that case, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) regarding the two properties to be proven—non-omniscience and non-authoritativeness—is doubtful.

(3/131) An example where the negative concomitance of the probans is doubtful is: "A certain person intended [by the opponent] is not one whose word is to be accepted among Brahmins learned in the three Vedas, because he possesses passion and so forth."

Here is an example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*): "Those whose words are authoritative are not possessed of passion and the like, such as Gautama and others, the authors of the Dharmaśāstras.
In this case, the exclusion of the property to be proven—possession of passion and the like—from Gautama and others is doubtful.
3/132 An example of doubtful exclusion of both [the property to be proved and the reason] is as follows: "Kapila and others were not free from passion, because they possessed attachment and grasping.
Here, the example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyeṇodāharaṇam*) is: "He who is free from passion does not possess attachment and grasping."
Regarding the phrase "as in the case of Ṛṣabha and others":

in the case of Ṛṣabha and others, because their lack of freedom from passion (*avītarāgatva*), as well as their possession of grasping and non-grasping, are [in doubt], the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) between the property to be proven (*sādhya*) and the proving property (*sādhana*) is doubtful.
(3/133) An example of a lack of negative concomitance (*avyatireka*) is: "This person is not free from passion, because he is a speaker."
An example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyeṇodāharaṇam*): "Wherever there is an absence of being free from passion, one is not a speaker;
for example, a piece of stone.

Although both [properties] are absent in the case of a piece of stone, nevertheless, because the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not established through the pervasion that "all those free from passion are not speakers," it is a fallacy of non-exclusion (*avyatireka*).
3/134 An example where the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not demonstrated: "Sound is impermanent because it is produced, like space," [stated] by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyeṇa*).
3/135 An example where the negative concomitance is inverted: "Whatever is unproduced is eternal.

3/136 For by means of these fallacious examples, it is not possible to demonstrate with certainty the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of the reason—that is, its presence only in similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and its absolute absence in all dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*)—nor its specific characteristic (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*).
Alternatively,
their refutation should be understood as resulting from the presumption of that [consequence]. 3/137 Refutation (*dūṣaṇa*) is the statement of deficiencies (*nyūnatā*) and so forth.
3/138 Refutation (*dūṣaṇa*) is the pointing out of those defects of the proof (*sādhana*), such as deficiency and so forth, which were previously mentioned;
for by that, the establishment of the opponent’s intended object is obstructed.
3/139 Fallacious refutations (*dūṣaṇābhāsa*), however, are the futile rejoinders (*jāti*).
"The pointing out of faults where none exist is called a futile rejoinder (jātyuttara).
Thus ends the third chapter, the Investigation of Inference for Others.
The treatise *Nyāyabindu* is completed.
